metadata.file_name: 3. Zhou et al. (2024). Investigating response behavior through TF-IDF and Word2vec text analysis_ A case study of PISA 2012 problem-solving process data.pdf
metadata.title: Investigating response behavior through TF-IDF and Word2vec text analysis: A case study of PISA 2012 problem-solving process data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the OECD PISA 2012 computer-based assessment process data for the “climate control (CP02501)” problem-solving task, sourced from the publicly available OECD database and the R ProcData package. The analytic dataset contains 16,763 preprocessed response behavior sequences, with “draw” removed and sequences binarized to correct (1) vs incorrect (0) based on scoring rules. The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling/student weights or any replicate-weight procedure (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and it does not mention weight variables (such as W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or complex survey design adjustments. Because the predictive models (KNN, SVM, Random Forest) are trained in Python (scikit-learn) without any stated weight-aware fitting, the analysis is treated as effectively unweighted; this may leave clustering/stratification effects unaccounted for in the ML stage.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values (PVs) are not applicable because the dependent variable is derived from PISA 2012 process-task scoring for the specific climate control item and is operationalized as a binary correctness outcome (0/1) from log-based task performance, not as a PV-based cognitive achievement score. The paper also does not describe any missing-data strategy for the process sequences (e.g., how incomplete logs or missing actions were handled), which represents a reporting gap given that log-based sequences can be incomplete or vary in length.
data.outcome_summary: The study evaluates TF-IDF and Word2vec feature extraction from PISA 2012 climate control process-response action sequences and then uses supervised ML to predict binary correctness (0/1). For logistic regression, Word2vec features slightly outperform TF-IDF (F1: 0.8224 vs 0.8169; Accuracy: 0.8017 vs 0.7993; Recall: 0.8360 vs 0.8149). For supervised prediction, Random Forest with TF-IDF is the best overall model (F1: 0.8419; Precision: 0.8271; Accuracy: 0.8231; Recall: 0.8572), outperforming Random Forest with Word2vec (F1: 0.8221; Accuracy: 0.8020; Recall: 0.8328). SVM performs better with Word2vec-derived features than with TF-IDF-derived features. In unsupervised clustering, k-means with TF-IDF yields three clusters with correct rates of 81%, 42%, and 36%, while k-means with Word2vec yields correct rates of 78%, 27%, and 26%; higher-accuracy clusters show higher VOTAT usage.
